lesson.title: NRZ Encoding: The Simplest Way to Draw a Bit
lesson.summary: Non-Return-to-Zero (NRZ) encoding maps each bit directly onto a signal level or a level change and holds it for the full bit period, which is bandwidth efficient but leaves clock recovery to solve on its own.
lesson.body:
NRZ, short for Non-Return-to-Zero, is close to the most direct encoding scheme you could design: hold the signal at one level for the entire duration of a bit, rather than forcing it back to some neutral zero level between bits the way some older telegraph era codes did, hence the name. There are two common variants, and the difference between them is exactly the difference between representing a bit as an absolute level versus representing it as a change. NRZ-L (Non-Return-to-Zero Level) assigns one voltage to a 1 and a different voltage to a 0 directly: whatever the current bit is, that is the level for the whole period. NRZ-I (Non-Return-to-Zero Invert) instead encodes a 1 as a transition at the start of the bit period and a 0 as no transition, so the receiver has to compare each bit's level to the previous bit's level rather than reading an absolute voltage.

Work through NRZ-L first, on the bit sequence 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, using a high voltage for 1 and a low voltage for 0. The signal is simply high, low, high, high, low, low, high, one flat level per bit period, with a transition only where consecutive bits actually differ. Compare that to NRZ-I on the same sequence, starting from an assumed initial low level: a 1 flips the level and a 0 holds it. Bit one (1) flips low to high; bit two (0) holds at high; bit three (1) flips high to low; bit four (1) flips low to high; bit five (0) holds at high; bit six (0) holds at high; bit seven (1) flips high to low. The resulting levels are high, high, low, high, high, high, low. Notice that NRZ-I only ever transitions on a 1, which makes it insensitive to which wire is which in a differential pair: if the two wires get swapped and every level inverts, the transitions, and therefore the decoded bits, are unaffected, which is part of why NRZ-I shows up in real interfaces like USB.

The shared weakness of both variants is the one the general encoding chapter already warned about. A long run of 1s in NRZ-L, or a long run of 0s in NRZ-I, produces a flat signal with no transitions at all for an entire stretch, starving a receiver's clock recovery circuit of anything to lock onto. Real systems that use NRZ variants at high speed almost always pair them with something else to guarantee transitions, such as scrambling the data to break up long runs, block codes like 8b/10b encoding that guarantee a minimum transition density, or simply an externally supplied clock signal alongside the data line.

Set against Manchester encoding from the previous chapter, the trade off is exactly the mirror image. NRZ needs roughly half the bandwidth of Manchester for the same bit rate, since it has at most one transition per bit period rather than the two that Manchester can require, but it gives up the guaranteed self clocking that Manchester provides for free. Which one a real system chooses depends on whether bandwidth or clocking simplicity is the scarcer resource on that particular link.
